    Column: ~How to Read & Roll Table Dice~
▼ D6
 This means "roll one die."
 The table entries correspond to the numbers 1 through 6, so
just check the result. Of course, you can also simply pick your
favorite!

▼ D66
 This means "roll two dice in order." The first die becomes
the tens digit, and the second die becomes the ones digit,
resulting in a two-digit number.
 For example, if your first die rolls a 2 and your second rolls
a 1, your result is "21"!
 Referring to the Wish Table on the previous page, a roll of 21
would correspond to "Pioneer of the Unknown."

▼☆
 This indicates that you roll two dice in order, with the first
die determining which row and the second die which column.
For instance, if your first die shows a 4 and your second die
shows a 2, your personality trait is "Airheaded."

name: Sample Synopses
text:
Sample Synopses
    In the sample synopses, each chapter and interlude includes a
  related title suggesting “how about this kind of role-play?”
    If you’re not yet familiar with TRPGs, these can help guide
  your role-playing. Even experienced players can use these tables
  as a reference when discussing what kind of role-play they want
  to try with their partner for the session.

  ▼ How to Use the Sample Synopses
    When the session begins, consult with your partner and
  choose one sample synopsis you like. Each sample contains vari-
  ous hints for setting up scenes and acting them out. Use the
  hints that appeal to you, skip the ones that don’t, and treat the
  sample as a flexible guide for your role-play.


       Heartfelt Animal Story
      [Chapter One] A scene where you’re unexpectedly befriended
      by an animal
        While the two of you are doing something (arguing, having a
      talk, shopping, etc.), an animal (a dog or cat works) comes up to
      you and, for some reason, takes a liking to you.
      [Chapter Two] A scene of bonding with the animal or reminisc-
      ing about the past
        This is a chance for characters to get sentimental. Maybe one
      has a special attachment to animals, or remembers a childhood
      pet.
      [Interlude] Now for the showdown
        For the sake of that animal who warmed up to you, you must
      protect Airceltrai. Steel your resolve and transform! For the two
      of you and your new companion!
      [Hints]
        Have the animal only warm up to one of the pair.
        Let one of the audience play the role of the animal.
      Try playing a character who’s actually afraid of animals, then
      gradually becomes friends with it.



128

Rules Section




 The Ground Hardens After a Rain
[Chapter One] Let’s have a fight! From the audience’s perspec-
tive, a quarrel between their favorites is a treat they can't
resist!
  Start a fight for some trivial (seriously small) reason. Maybe the
room’s a mess, one forgot a promise, or one got caught eyeing a
cute passerby.
[Chapter Two] Be awkward
  The next day, you’re together but there’s distance. Maybe you
avoid each others eyes, or force yourselves to act like you’re still
fighting even though you’re really close. Lay it on thick!
[Interlude] Then apologize
  Make up with each other. A little tsundere attitude is perfect. As
a bonus, make a promise for after the Stellar Battle, maybe go
shopping or treat the other to a meal.
[Hints]
  The reason for the fight should be trivial (but important to the
characters). If it’s too serious, you might not be able to wrap it up
in three scenes!




 Rainy Day
[Chapter One] Let it rain
  A scene by the window, gazing at the rain. Maybe you had plans
to go out, or you’re wondering if it’ll clear up by tomorrow, chat
about the weather. You’ll naturally end up alone together in the
same room!
[Chapter Two] Since the rain won’t stop, let's get cozy at home
  Try cooking together, or have a flashback scene about your
shared past. For flashbacks, “I always remember old times on
rainy days” is a classic go-to line!
[Interlude]
  Make a promise for what you’ll do on the next sunny day!
[Hints]
  The phrase “The rain won’t let up, huh?” is almost too handy. If
there’s five seconds of silence, talk about the rain. It’s also a good
idea to link the characters’ emotions to the weather; when their
worries clear up, maybe the skies clear as well!



                                                                         129
